deep.reconstruction:
This page continues a lecture-style exposition from the previous folio. That folio derived the conservation of vis viva for central and mutual forces, (1/2)Σ m v^2 − (1/2)Σ m v0^2 = P − P0, and the corollary that the total work of all forces is 0 when the masses return to their initial relative positions. It then began a historical account of the mechanical theory of heat (Davy 1799, Mayer 1842). There are no derivations on this page; it is historical and physical commentary.

(1) Joule's result. Joule showed that the heat produced by friction is proportional to the mechanical work consumed. After experiments in 1843, 1845 and 1848, he stated in 1850: 'the quantity of heat that raises 1 lb of water by 1 °F requires the expenditure of a mechanical force able to raise 772.692 lb by one foot.' In modern terms, J ≈ 772.692 ft·lbf per (lb·°F).

Riemann lists Joule's three friction values:
- water: 772.692
- mercury: 774.083
- cast iron: 774.987

These agree to within about 0.3%. Riemann concludes that the foundation of the mechanical theory of heat is experimentally established.

(2) The principle being tested. The principle is that the total work W of unknown (molecular) forces is 0 whenever all material particles between which those forces act return to the same relative configuration. That is, the work is a closed-loop integral over a cyclic process: ∮ Σ (X dx + Y dy + Z dz) = 0.

Riemann's logic: heat is the vis viva of molecular motion (marginal note on the previous page). So equivalence of heat and consumed work, independent of material and process, confirms that the molecular forces do zero net work over a cycle.

(3) Electrical case. Joule produced a galvanic current by equal forces and used it in very different ways, either to produce heat or to do mechanical work. In every case, mechanical work consumed plus the mechanical equivalent of the heat produced was the same. Hence the work done by the molecular forces between electricity and ponderable matter, and between the electric particles themselves, must also be 0 when the current stops and the conductors return to their former state.

The next page completes the argument:
- the perpetuum-mobile argument;
- path independence of the work integral, hence the existence of a potential;
- conservation of actual plus potential energy (Helmholtz's 'Spannkräfte').
errors: No mathematical errors. The numerical values match Joule's 1850 Phil. Trans. paper (water 772.692, mercury 774.083, cast iron 774.987 ft·lb).

The experiment years '1843, 45, 48' are slightly loose. Joule's main series were 1843 (magneto-electric and water-through-tubes), 1845, and 1847 (paddle wheel), with publication in 1850. Joule's own summary statement rounded the figure to 772 lb.

The page attributes to Joule experiments in which electrical work was used variously for heat or mechanical work. This is broadly correct (Joule 1841–1843 on heating by currents, and the magneto-electric engine), but the description is schematic.

results.what: Mechanical equivalent of heat, ≈ 772.7 ft·lbf per lb·°F, nearly the same for water, mercury and cast iron
results.usually_credited_to: J. P. Joule (1843–1850); also J. R. Mayer (1842)

results.what: Zero total work of molecular and electrical forces over a cyclic process, viewed as experimentally confirmed by heat–work equivalence
results.modern_name: First law of thermodynamics / conservation of energy (conservative forces, path-independence of work)

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard lecture notes on the history and experimental basis of energy conservation. They faithfully quote Joule's published 1850 values; nothing is original or unexpected.

checkable.asserts: Converts Joule's 772.692 ft·lbf/Btu to ≈4.157 J/cal, i.e. about 0.7% below the modern 4.1868.
The spread between the cast iron and water values is ≈0.30%.
The spread between the mercury and water values is ≈0.18%.
Joule's value in SI is ≈4153 J per kg·K, compared with the modern specific heat of water ≈4184 J/(kg·K).

transcription_corrections: Line 3: 'ein Wasser' should read 'ein lb Wasser' (one pound of water); the 'lb' symbol is visible in the image.
'772,692 lb um einen Fuss zu heben' is correct; the closing quote mark follows 'heben'.
The insertion near 'war in allen Fällen gleich gross' reads 'in der Kette' (in the circuit); the transcription marks this as uncertain, and the reading is plausible.

Last paragraph, intended reading after deletions: 'Es musste also die von den Molecularkräften zwischen der Electricität und den Stofftheilchen und von den [Kräften] zwischen den electrischen Theilchen geleistete Arbeit = 0 sein, wenn der galvanische Strom aufhört und die Leiter ihren vorigen Zustand wieder annehmen.'
